topic: Definition of done and acceptance criteria distinction
query: definition of done criterion software engineering acceptance criteria
title: Definition of Done vs Acceptance Criteria
snippet: Acceptance criteria are unique to a specific user story or backlog item, while the definition of done applies universally to all. Acceptance criteria define what a feature is supposed to do, while the definition of done indicates what is required for the feature to be considered ready for release.
claim: Acceptance criteria are story-specific requirements while the definition of done is a universal quality gate applying to all work.

topic: Acceptance criteria as testable verification conditions
title: Acceptance Criteria in Agile Testing - TestRail
snippet: Acceptance tests are the actual verification that the acceptance criteria have been met, checking whether expected behavior exists in the working software. They are executable and can be run manually by a QA engineer or automated using a test framework, producing a result of pass or fail.
claim: Acceptance criteria verification requires executable tests that can be run manually or automated, producing measurable pass/fail outcomes.

topic: Boolean invariant verification in CI/CD systems
query: boolean invariant verification CI/CD pipeline testing
title: Securing the agentic era: Introducing formal verification for CEL
snippet: Assertions and assumptions define the boundaries of acceptable behavior, allowing developers to configure CI/CD pipelines to validate changes simply and securely. An invariant 'universal_no_unapproved_privileged_prod' violation can be detected, showing how boolean conditions can be formally verified within automated pipelines.
claim: Boolean invariants can be formally verified within CI/CD pipelines to validate that system properties and constraints are maintained.

topic: In-toto attestation framework and DSSE structure
title: In-Toto Attestations - Sigstore
snippet: The in-toto Attestation Framework provides a specification for generating verifiable claims about any aspect of how a piece of software is produced. DSSE (Dead Simple Signing Envelope) is a standard JSON format for signing arbitrary data that contains a payload, its type, and digital signatures. The specification for in-toto attestations can be broken down to three layers: the DSSE Envelope (the transport layer), the in-toto Statement (the attestation header), and the predicate (the attestation payload).
claim: In-toto attestations use DSSE envelopes to wrap signed claims about software production, with three layers: transport envelope, statement header, and predicate payload.

title: Attestation in Cybersecurity: Types, Uses & Best Practices
snippet: Attestation evidence contains claims about the physical characteristics and the configuration settings of the execution environment. Examples include CPU manufacturer, model and version, microcode and firmware version, and configuration settings such as whether memory encryption is enabled. The values supplied in the attestation evidence are compared against reference values.
claim: Configuration attestation verifies that actual environment characteristics match declared reference values for security and compliance.

topic: Test breakage detection in staged testing
query: staged testing breakage detection software quality
title: A Systematic Literature Review of Test Breakage Prevention and Repair Techniques
snippet: Early test breakage detection systems use presubmit runs, maintaining a representation of recent test history for each combination of a test and build flags, including both presubmit results for pending changes and postsubmit results for submitted changes, to determine the cause of test breakage.
claim: Early breakage detection requires maintaining test history across flag combinations to distinguish code failures from test infrastructure problems.

topic: SLSA provenance and definition of done
query: SLSA provenance definition of done supply chain
title: SLSA (Supply-chain Levels for Software Artifacts) What is it?
snippet: SLSA, short for Supply-chain Levels for Software Artifacts, is a software supply chain security framework designed to improve build integrity, provenance, and trust in software artifacts. The framework is organized into tracks and levels; the build track has four levels (L0–L3) representing increasing grades of security, from no provenance at L0 to a hardened, isolated build platform with authenticated, signed provenance at L3.
claim: SLSA levels L1-L3 provide progressively stronger provenance guarantees from basic attestation through hosted builds to isolated platforms with signed claims.

title: Integrating Formal Verification and Simulation-based Assertion Checking in a Corroborative V&V Process
snippet: Properties are extracted from requirements and formally verified at the design level, while verified properties are propagated to the implementation level and checked via testing. Evidence generated by one V&V process supports evidence generated by the others, and when taken together, confidence in the overall safety is improved.
claim: Corroborative verification integrates formal proofs and simulation testing so evidence from each process reinforces the other.
